source.title: Practice with Sleep Makes Perfect: Sleep-Dependent Motor Skill Learning

confidence_rationale: The foundational, most-cited paper establishing that sleep -- specifically the amount of stage-2 NREM late in the night -- drives overnight motor sequence gains that equivalent wake time does not. Included as the canonical anchor the later chunk-concatenation work refines, and as independent, large-effect, well-replicated confirmation of the NREM2-not-REM stage attribution. Held at moderate rather than high confidence because it measures whole-sequence speed and accuracy (a coarser index than the later chunk-transition-specific work) and does not itself distinguish chunk formation from execution fluency -- that refinement came from the later papers, not this one.
failure_signatures: The outcome measure is overall sequence typing speed and accuracy, not a transition-level or chunk-level breakdown -- this paper alone cannot distinguish 'sleep formed better chunks' from 'sleep made execution of the same chunks more fluent,' the exact distinction MECH-490 needs; that separation is only available from the later Bottary/Blischke work.

A finger-keypress sequence task, learned to criterion via massed practice in a single session, then retested after one night -- a much shorter and simpler learning/consolidation window than a Fishtank agent's ongoing, environment-conditioned replanning.

Some later studies (e.g. Rickard et al. 2008, cited widely as a partial non-replication for probabilistic sequence learning) found sleep benefits were smaller or absent for less deterministic sequence structures -- this paper's finding is robust for a fixed, deterministic sequence but should not be over-generalised to all motor-sequence learning without qualification.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Participants trained on a five-element finger-tapping sequence showed no significant improvement across a 12-hour waking retention interval, but a 20.5% speed improvement (without loss of accuracy) across a 12-hour interval containing a night of sleep. The magnitude of overnight improvement correlated significantly with the percentage of stage-2 NREM sleep obtained, particularly in the last quarter of the night (r=0.72, p=0.008), with no significant correlation to REM sleep amount.
mapping.ree_translation: REE reads this as the foundational precedent establishing that human motor-sequence consolidation is sleep-dependent and specifically NREM2-linked rather than REM-linked -- the same stage attribution the later, more granular chunk-concatenation work (Bottary et al. 2016) converges on for the fluency-specific sub-phenomenon MECH-490 targets. Taken together with that later work, this paper strengthens the claim's depends_on finding that MECH-204's REM-phase route is unlikely to be the correct biological analogue for a sleep-linked coherence effect, if one exists in the Fishtank data.
mapping.mapping_caveat: This paper cannot itself discriminate formation from fluency -- it is cited as background/foundational support for the NREM2-not-REM direction, not as direct evidence for the specific commit-gate-persistence mechanism, which the more granular Bottary/Blischke entries address more precisely. Treat as corroborating context, not as primary evidence for MECH-490's specific mechanistic claim.
mapping.source_context: Healthy young adults, laboratory finger-tapping sequence task, within-subject sleep-vs-wake retention comparison, polysomnography-recorded sleep-stage composition, single-session acquisition.

confidence_components.notes: Source quality very high (Neuron, foundational, >1000 citations, tight within-subject design). Mapping fidelity moderate-low specifically because this paper cannot separate formation from fluency -- the distinction MECH-490 is built around -- so it grounds the general NREM2 stage attribution but not the mechanism-specific claim. Included as corroborating canonical context rather than the primary evidentiary basis.
